2. Diagram Component Palette

Click elements to instantiate them onto the architecture canvas window.

Process / Service
Process Component
Functional Definition:
Any active computational engine, runtime application container, execution node, or microservice block running business instructions software.
Data Store
Data Store Component
Functional Definition:
Any persistence layer, ledger engine, cluster directory, hardware disk partition, or caching cluster storing persistent or volatile system state data.
External Entity
External Entity Component
Functional Definition:
An untrusted origin consumer, client terminal, or downstream partner framework sitting outside system cluster firewall configurations.
Trust Boundary Zone
Trust Boundary Zone
Functional Definition:
A structural border isolation box grouping items together where privilege access levels or trust shifting context boundaries change.
Trust Boundary Line
Trust Boundary Line
Functional Definition:
A linear segment indicating a change in trust, privilege levels, or security protocols between distinct architectural layers.

Step Activity
Step Activity Component
Functional Definition:
An indexable timeline sequence node used to illustrate sequential activities, data flows, or multi-step user interaction journeys.
Comment Textbox
Comment Textbox
Functional Definition:
A documentation utility block to add descriptive metadata, assumptions, or operational context notes onto specific canvas regions.
Canvas Headline
Canvas Headline
Functional Definition:
A stylized text display label used to organize architecture charts into clear visual blocks or create master banners.

Custom Image / Icon
Custom Graphic Image
Functional Definition:
Allows importing custom graphic elements, system logos, or specific icons directly onto the diagram. Supports loading local files or web URLs.
Infrastructure Node
Infrastructure Component
Functional Definition:
Any physical or virtual hardware server, security appliance, network switch, router, firewall, or email broker mapping infrastructure layers.

Swimlane Grid Layout
Swimlane Grid Layout
Functional Definition:
A dynamic matrix grid component that automatically groups, bounds, and resizes relative to elements placed inside its cells. Supports adding/deleting rows and columns.
Process (Rectangle)
□ Process (Rectangle)
Flowchart Definition:
Represents a step or action in a process. The standard rectangular symbol used for any general operation or task.
Decision (Diamond)
◆ Decision (Diamond)
Flowchart Definition:
Represents a decision point with branching paths (Yes/No, True/False). A diamond shape indicating a conditional check.
Terminator (Oval)
◯ Terminator (Oval)
Flowchart Definition:
Marks the Start or End point of a process flow. A rounded stadium/pill shape used at the beginning and termination of a flowchart.
Data / I-O
▱ Data / I-O
Flowchart Definition:
Represents input or output data. A parallelogram indicating data entering or leaving a process step.
Document
📄 Document
Flowchart Definition:
Represents a document or report produced or used by a process. Has a rectangular top and a wavy bottom edge.
Manual Input
▩ Manual Input
Flowchart Definition:
Represents a step where data is manually entered by a person. A trapezoid with a slanted top edge indicating keyboard or form input.
Preparation (Hexagon)
⬡ Preparation
Flowchart Definition:
Represents initialization or preparatory steps, such as setting a loop counter. A hexagon with pointed left and right sides.
Connector (Circle)
◯ Connector
Flowchart Definition:
A small circle used as an on-page or off-page connector to link separate sections of a flowchart, avoiding long crossing lines.
Stored Data
⌨ Stored Data
Flowchart Definition:
Represents data stored somewhere in a system — on disk, memory, or a file. A rounded-right D-shaped symbol.
Database (Cylinder)
🖽 Database (Cylinder)
Flowchart Definition:
Represents a database or structured data store with a 3D cylindrical appearance. Common in system/architecture diagrams.
Cube (3D Box)
Cube (3D Box)
Flowchart Definition:
A three-dimensional box, for a server, a container, a package or any other physical or deployable unit. Common in system/architecture diagrams.

Help & License v
1. How Threat Tiger works

Threat modeling means looking at how a system is built and asking "what could go wrong?" before attackers do. In Threat Tiger you draw the system as a data-flow diagram — processes, data stores, external entities (users and outside systems) and the data flows between them — and mark trust boundaries where data moves between areas with different levels of trust, such as from the internet into your network.

For each part of the diagram you then consider the six STRIDE threat categories. Each one is the opposite of a security property you want to keep:

  • Spoofing (authentication): someone pretends to be another user, service or device.
  • Tampering (integrity): data, code or configuration is changed by someone who should not change it.
  • Repudiation (accountability): someone can deny having done something because there is no reliable record.
  • Information Disclosure (confidentiality): data is exposed to people or systems that should not see it.
  • Denial of Service (availability): the system is slowed down or stopped for legitimate users.
  • Elevation of Privilege (authorization): someone gains more rights than they were given.

Select a component and open Threat Templates for ideas. Set the security switches in Properties (for example "encrypted" or "stores PII") and draw trust boundaries: Threat Tiger then suggests threats that follow from your design. The icon and name of a component also count: a component drawn as a GPU server, a .env file or a WordPress site gets threats for that kind of component. Record the threats that apply in the register, rate them by likelihood and impact, and track how they are mitigated. The Insights tab lists every open suggestion (filter by component, STRIDE category or reason) and shows what is still uncovered.

Flowcharts and swimlanes
  • Quick add: hover a connection point of a flowchart shape to see a preview of the next step; click to add it, already connected. Drag from the point to connect to an existing node instead.
  • Change type: use Type in Properties to turn any node into another kind (process, data store, decision, …). Name, flows and threats stay.
  • Swimlanes: drop a node into a cell (it is highlighted while you drag); cells grow to fit their nodes. Drag a column or row border to resize it, double-click it for the automatic size, and pick a colour in Properties.
  • Align and distribute: select two or more shapes to line them up or space them evenly from the small toolbar above the canvas controls.
  • Minimap: turn it on from ☰ menu → Show minimap. It shows the whole diagram in the top-right corner of the canvas; click or drag in it to move the view.
  • Format painter: select a shape, click the brush, then click another shape of the same kind to copy its colours (not its name, type or security settings). Double-click the brush to paint several; Esc stops.
  • Line jumps: where two flows cross, the later one hops over the other; switch it off in ☰ menu → Line jumps where flows cross. Bend points: click a selected flow to add one, drag to move, click to remove, or use Clear bend points in Properties.
  • Layers: in the left column, add layers, click one to make it active (new shapes go there), double-click to rename, hide or lock it, or move the selection to it. Hidden layers still count in the threat analysis.
  • Mermaid: ☰ menu → Import Mermaid flowchart… turns a flowchart into shapes, flows and trust zones (from subgraphs).
